name: 'Amir ibn at-Tufail
bio: 'Amir ibn at-Tufail, nephew of Mu'awiyah ibn Malik, was the famous cavalier and contemporary of the Prophet who was chief of the tribe of 'Amir ibn Sa'sa'ah. Lyall edited his Diwan in 1913.
Ode CVI is No. XI of the Diwan; the second piece is a rejoinder to Salamah ibn al-Khurshub.

poems.title: Ode CVI: Of a truth the Chiefs of
poems.author: 'Amir ibn at-Tufail
poems.note: Lyall's heading: 'Amir son of at-Tufail, of Ja'far, of Kilab, of 'Amir ibn Sa'sa'ah.
poems.text:
Of a truth the Chiefs of Hawazin know well that I am the knight who defends the cause of the House of Ja'far ;

And al-Maznuq too knows well that I urged him again and again against the enemy's host, as one puts back into the bag again and again the blank arrow, denounced by the gamers.

When he flinched and turned aside from the thrust of the spears, I pressed him onwards and said — ' Get thee on, straight forward — never turn thy back ! '

And I admonished him that to fly were a disgrace for a man so long as he has not put forth his utmost strength and done all possible to him :

' Seest thou not that their spears are all couched straight at me ? and thou art a charger of noble stock : so bear it bravely ! '

I desired that God might know that I endured patiently : and in truth I dreaded a day like the Day of al-Mushaqqar !

By my life ! — and my life is no light thing to me — verily the spear-thrust of Mus-hir has spoiled the beauty of my face !

And a wretched man shall I be if I be one-eyed, unsteady on my legs, a coward — and what shall be my excuse in all assemblies ?

And sooth, they know full well that I dashed again and again against them, on the evening of Faif ar-Rih, as one circles time after time the standing Pillar ;

And I ceased not until my throat and my charger's breast were covered with streaming blood, like the fringe of a striped silken cloth.

I say to a soul the like of which is not poured forth [in death]: 'Cut short thine exulting ! verily I fail not in carrying out my purpose :

'Yea, if they had been a host like ourselves in number, we had not cared for them : but there came upon us an overwhelming mass, full of boastful words —

'They came upon us with the cavalry of all the broad plain, and the whole of Aklub, clad in leather cuirasses.'

poems.title: Ode CVII: Now let Asma ask — for
poems.author: 'Amir ibn at-Tufail
poems.text:
Now let Asma ask — for she is kind and cares for our fortunes — let her ask her counsellors whether I was driven away or not.

They said to her — 'Yea, we drove away and scattered his horsemen'. The yellow-toothed dogs ! it was not I that was wont to be driven away !

And I will surely proclaim your disgraceful doings at al-Mala and 'Uwarid, and I will bring my horses down upon you at the Lava of Darghad —

The horses that stumble among the broken spear-shafts, looking like kites following one another in the straight way !

And I will surely take vengeance for Malik, and for Malik, and for the man of al-Maraurat whose head was not propped in his grave !

And the man whom Hurrah slew will I surely avenge — truly he was a noble chief : their brother [for whom they slew him] was not killed.

O Asma, thou child of the House of Fazarah, a fighter am I, and no man can hope to live for ever !

Get thee gone to thine own ! No peace can there be between us, after the knights that lie dead in the place of ambush, —

Save by the help of black, tall, swimming steeds, and the comfort that comes from the thrust of a tawny spear !

A child of War am I : I cease not to heighten her blaze by night, and light her up to burn whensoever she is not yet kindled.
